blocks.content: The Docker daemon (dockerd) is the background process that does all the real work: it builds images, starts and stops containers, and manages networks and volumes. Every client request eventually lands here.

Think of the daemon as the kitchen behind the client's waiter. It owns every image on the host, every container (running or stopped), every Docker network, and every volume. Nothing happens to any of those resources without going through the daemon first.

blocks.alt: The daemon owns every image, container, network and volume

blocks.content: 2. It Serves Many Clients at Once
blocks.text: 2. It Serves Many Clients at Once

blocks.content: A single daemon is not tied to a single client session. Your terminal, a CI pipeline, and Docker Desktop can all be issuing requests to the same daemon simultaneously, and it processes them all against the same shared state.

blocks.alt: One daemon, many clients, one shared state

blocks.content: 3. The Daemon Does Not Do Everything Alone
blocks.text: 3. The Daemon Does Not Do Everything Alone

blocks.content: Modern Docker splits responsibilities further under the hood: dockerd delegates the actual container execution work to containerd, which in turn hands off to runc to do the low-level work of creating the isolated process. This layering is covered in depth in the Docker Internals module, for now, just know that "the daemon does the work" is a useful simplification, not the full picture.

blocks.alt: The daemon delegates the lowest-level work further down

blocks.content: The daemon keeps a running record of what exists: which containers are up, which are stopped, what networks they are attached to. Every docker ps or docker inspect is really just the daemon reporting back its own internal bookkeeping.

blocks.alt: The daemon is the source of truth for what is actually running

blocks.content: 5. Starting and Stopping the Daemon Itself
blocks.text: 5. Starting and Stopping the Daemon Itself

blocks.content: On a Linux server, the daemon usually runs as a system service, started at boot by systemd. If docker commands suddenly start failing with a connection error, checking whether the daemon itself is alive is the very first debugging step.

blocks.alt: systemd is typically what keeps dockerd running

blocks.content:
sudo systemctl status docker
sudo systemctl restart docker
# If the daemon is down, every docker command will fail
# with something like "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon".

code.content:
sudo systemctl status docker
sudo systemctl restart docker
# If the daemon is down, every docker command will fail
# with something like "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon".

codes.bash:
sudo systemctl status docker
sudo systemctl restart docker
# If the daemon is down, every docker command will fail
# with something like "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon".

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: The daemon is where the actual work happens: building images, running containers, managing networks and volumes, and tracking the live state of all of them.
If Docker commands stop responding, check the daemon itself first, everything else (client, registry, images) depends on it being alive.
